items.title: A protein that teaches cells to tolerate DNA damage points to a new vulnerability in cancer
items.text: Cancer begins in DNA, which is why everything about this well-known molecule is extensively studied at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO). For instance, what exactly happens when DNA is duplicated? Every time a cell divides into two daughter cells, its DNA is copied. Researchers at CNIO and Stanford University have now uncovered a new aspect of this complex process, which has been studied for decades but still holds many surprises.

items.title: Experimental drug shows promise in overcoming treatment resistance in aggressive acute myeloid leukemia
items.text: Researchers at the Johns Hopkins Sidney Kimmel Comprehensive Cancer Center and Johns Hopkins Children's Center found that an experimental drug may help overcome one of the major challenges in treating an aggressive subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), known as FLT3-positive AML. In laboratory and animal studies, the drug, called PHI-101, was effective against leukemia cells carrying genetic mutations that cause resistance to existing FLT3-targeted therapies.

items.title: A forgotten organ sheds new light on the origins of the ovary
items.text: How do ovaries develop? Much remains unknown. By studying the "rete ovarii," a small anatomical structure that has long been overlooked, a team at the University of Geneva (UNIGE) has uncovered the dual origin of the cells that surround and protect oocytes. This discovery offers new insights into ovarian development and opens up new avenues for research into fertility and gynecological cancers.
